El Monumento Arqueológico de Sillustani es uno de los complejos funerarios más impresionantes del altiplano peruano. Ubicado a orillas de la laguna Umayo, combina historia, arquitectura y paisajes únicos. Lo visité un lunes y practicamente fuimos los unicos turistas por lo que pudimos recorrer y tomarnos fotos con total tranquilidad. La entrada cuesta 15 soles, el recorrido esta señalizado y te demora entre una hora y media a 2 horas.  En este lugar se encuentran las famosas Chullpas, torres funerarias construidas por las culturas Kolla y posteriormente por los Incas. Destacan por su arquitectura de piedras perfectamente talladas y ensambladas con una precisión sorprendente, especialmente la Chullpa del Lagarto, una de las más representativas.  El recorrido permite conocer la tradición funeraria prehispánica, apreciar diversas estructuras de distintas épocas y disfrutar de una vista espectacular del lago y el entorno natural. Es un sitio ideal para quienes buscan cultura, historia y conexión con el paisaje andino.  Muy recomendable visitarlo pero llevar bloqueador y gorra ya que  el sol es implacable. Un lugar imperdible en Puno.

About 20 km northwest of Puno, on a peninsula in Laguna Umayo, lies the remarkable pre-Inca cemetery of Sillustani. The tombs, tower-like structures called chullpas, are the tangible remnant of the burial culture of the Qulla people, a people conquered by the Inca Empire in the 15th century. Entire family groups were buried in the chullpas; these tombs were most likely reserved for the nobility. A fascinating destination!

Absolutely breathtaking! Visiting Sillustani is like stepping back in time. The ancient chullpas, or funerary towers, stand proudly on a peninsula with a stunning panoramic view of Lake Umayo. The craftsmanship of these structures is incredible, and the historical significance of the Colla and Inca civilizations is palpable. The atmosphere is mystical and peaceful, making it a perfect spot for reflection and photography. Just be prepared for the high altitude and cool winds—bring warm clothing! It's a must-see on any trip from Puno and a truly unforgettable experience.

L'île Amantani à une superficie de 9,28 km2, et une population de 3 663 habitants répartis en 800 familles. Elle est parfois appelée « île du Kantuta », parce qu'on y trouve en abondance la Cantua buxifolia, que la Bolivie et le Pérou ont choisi comme plante-emblème. L'île dispose de deux pics, le Pachatata (la "terre de père") et le Pachamama (la "terre mère"), avec des ruines Inca et Tiwanaku sur leur sommet. Les collines sont en terrasses principalement travaillées à la main et plantées de blé, de quinoa, de pommes de terre et d'autres légumes.

ISLA APACIBLE Y PARTE DEL RECORRIDO A LAS ISLAS DE LOS UROS  La isla de Amantaní, perteneciente al distrito del mismo nombre en la Región de Puno, Perú, se encuentra al este de la península de Capachica [4.4 km], y al norte de la isla de Taquile [8.1 km], en el Lago Titicaca.  La ocupación de la isla se remonta ya a la época pre Inca. Por los años 1580 la isla fue vendida por el Rey Carlos V al español Pedro González.  Desde ese momento la isla estuvo en manos de los gamonales descendientes de los españoles. A comienzos del 1900, como consecuencia de las fuertes sequías, los hacendados comenzaron a vender las tierras a los nativos.

這是一個可愛的小島，我們住在這裡，民宿的爸爸，媽媽非常和善，晚餐，早餐都讓我很滿足，比較可惜的是民宿的房間沒有衛浴設備，只能大家一起共用一個洗手間🚻有點不太方便，也不方便洗澡，房間沒有插座無法充電真的很不方便，網路🛜是幾乎都沒有訊號，過了一天與世隔絕的日子，  我爬上了這裡的置高景點，看到美麗的夕陽覺得很值得，也鍛練自己的體能，  Taquile Island 因為島上的手工藝而在 2005 年被 UNESCO 世界遺產 認證為 “非物質文化遺產代表作 Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity”  這個島的婦女都很會編織毛衣及毛帽，手套，我跟民宿的媽媽捧場買了一頂毛帽子，因為覺得手工細緻，織工特別，又聽聞媽媽說是一針一線織了一個月才完工，沒有想到我戴上這頂毛帽子 一直被詢問我買了多少錢？很多人都很好奇，連到了Puno鎮車站的小販也詢問我價格？也聽說只有那個小島才有販售，而且不外銷，很慶幸我買了它，就當作是一個紀念品吧！  聽聞這邊的男人跟一般南美洲的男人不一樣, 他們8歲就需要開始用羊毛針織, 連娶老婆都是要看針織的帽子能不能細密到滴水不漏才能娶回家. 很多娶了隔壁村的老婆，也有城市嫁到這個島上的。  自助旅行者的幸福感：找到快樂的泉源，發現與眾不同

A experiência de se hospedar em uma casa de família local é algo inesquecível e enriquecedor. Aprender de perto sobre os costumes e tradições de povos tão antigos é inexplicável. No entanto, esse tipo de vivência não é pra todo o tipo de turista. Ao chegarmos na ilha, somos divididos em grupos de 4 para nos hospedarmos na casa de uma família. As casas são simples, sem calefação,(fomos em setembro e fazia muito frio), o banheiro não tem chuveiro e o cheiro que vinha dele não era dos melhores. A família que nos recebeu é muito acolhedora e simpática. À tarde, depois de aprendermos sobre os costumes locais, caminhamos para o ponto mais alto da ilha afim de ver os templos de pachatata e pachamama, além de assistir o lindo pôr do sol no lago Titicaca. Essa caminhada não foi fácil pois a altitude afeta bastante nosso fôlego. À noite, nos vestiram com trajes locais para uma festa divertida com todos os turistas na ilha. No dia seguinte tomamos café e partimos.

First, let me tell you that those people don't really live on Uros Islands, it's just a show. We confirmed that by staying overnight and also talking with locals in Puno. The only people that stay there overnight are people that rent out lodges.  It's a tourist trap, if you go on a tour it's just a giant sales pitch where they try to sell you souvenirs you can buy in puno 80% cheaper. Of course they claim they made them themselves.  The lodge that we rented turned out to be twice the price because we had to pay 100 soles for the transfer in that tiny boat in the picture. For reference, organized 3h tours from Puno are 20 soles, and if you go directly to the "harbor" you can find them for 10. Plus you pay 5 soles per person for the lake entry tickets, and then if you want dinner, it's set menu of children meal size that is 40 soles per person (12 soles in Puno).  My advice is to go and visit if it's your bucket list thing, but don't feel obliged to buy anything, they're literally scammers that use the opportunistic business practices and isolated location to squeeze anything they can from you.

The Uros Islands (Islas de los Uros) on Lake Titicaca are a truly unique cultural and natural experience. These floating islands are made entirely of totora reeds, which the Uros people have used for centuries to build their homes, boats, and the islands themselves. Visiting gives you a fascinating glimpse into their traditional way of life, while also showing how they balance heritage with modern tourism.  The islands are small and can feel quite tourist-oriented, but the hospitality of the local families is warm, and the setting on the high-altitude lake is breathtaking. A boat ride on a traditional reed boat adds to the charm. It’s best visited with an open mind, appreciating both the cultural showcase for visitors and the resilience of the community.  Ideal for travelers interested in indigenous culture, history, and unique landscapes.

The Uros (or Uru) are one of the oldest peoples of the Andes who today mainly live around Lake Titicaca, Lake Poopó and along the Rio Lauca. The best known group are the Uros who live on the floating islands in Lake Titicaca near Puno, Peru. With the arrival of the Incas, the Uros, who lived mainly from hunting and fishing, fled to Lake Titicaca where they built and still build their famous floating islands from the thick blocks of totora reed roots. The totora reed is a building material by the Uros on the one hand, they not only make their islands from it, but also their huts and boats, and on the other hand the white underside of the reed is eaten (and is therefore a source of iodine). Where the Uros used to have to live from hunting and fishing, a difficult life that did not generate a particularly high income, nowadays tourism is an important source of income. An educational excursion, the sale of souvenirs and even an overnight stay are possible. The floating islands: a fun and unique destination!

Taquile Island, on Lake Titicaca, is a peaceful and scenic destination known for its rich cultural traditions. Unlike the smaller Uros Islands, Taquile feels less commercial and offers a more authentic glimpse of daily life. The island is famous for its handwoven textiles, recognized by UNESCO, and you’ll often see locals dressed in traditional clothing that reflects their community roles.  The views from the island are stunning, with terraced hillsides overlooking the deep blue lake. Be prepared for some hiking, as reaching the main square involves climbing many stone steps at high altitude—but the panorama is well worth it. Life here is slow-paced, making it a wonderful place to disconnect and experience Andean culture.  A great choice for travelers who enjoy cultural immersion, local crafts, and natural beauty.
